utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just to place on record that, once again, Judge Orie is not with us because of urgent Tribunal business, and, therefore, Judge Fluegge and I have decided to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis in the interests of justice. Thank you so much. May we please move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Good morning, Witness RM314. Just to remind you that you're still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you, too. And I stand by my oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. RM314. Mr. Ivetic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. I'd like to start by calling up another document that should not be broadcast. It's 1D948. Sir, while we wait for the document I believe it is a medical document dated the 16th of July, 1995. And when it comes up, I would ask you to take a look at it and verify that you recognise this as being the document from your first -- one of your first medical examinations when you arrived at the free Bosnian Muslim territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour, it should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is correct. This is my first diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now looking at the line item for your profession, this document lists you as being a soldier, does this accord with what you told the people at the clinic about your status on this date?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was admitted to the Gradina Medical Centre because all other facilities were occupied. We were told that we had to move to the Gradina infirmary and they emptied four rooms in order to put in all the wounded from the -- Srebrenica. So this document was issued by the garrison infirmary where I was hospitalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for that information. And then my question was: Did you in fact -- or does -- does the occupation of soldier accord with what you told the staff at the clinic your status was?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say anything. I was a civilian ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part. We did not understand what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, the interpreters didn't hear the last part of your answer. Could you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody asked me whether I was a soldier or not. And it wasn't me who dictated this certificate. That means that the person who issued this certificate is responsible for its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The certificate also says: "Wounded four days ago while escaping from Srebrenica. And were wounded in the left hip area." Does this accord with the description of how and when you were wounded that you gave to the medical staff at the clinic?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I provided the details as to where I was wounded, in which hip, and they received it from the medical centre. So based on the wound, they compiled this diagnosis sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And looking further on the sheet, at least the English translation indicates that you're performing messenger or courier duties at the Srebrenica prime school. Is this in fact correct or not?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask you to look at the B/C/S original, there's listed for the place of your employment the OS Srebrenica in Bosnian. Would you agree with me that OS Srebrenica can refer also to the armed forces of Srebrenica, the "oruzane snage"?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The defence department was part of the civilian authorities, not the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. I'm talking about the abbreviation OS in the Bosnian original. OS Srebrenica, that abbreviation could stand for armed forces Srebrenica. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to you, yes. But I was a courier for the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document under seal as the next Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 1D948 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D948 receives number D282, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Registrar. Under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, in the English the diagnosis is -- is listed as not being legible, but it is in the handwritten B/C/S original. We see it there. I want to ask you -- I know it's in Latin, so I want to just ask you: Did anyone at the clinic explain for you what their diagnoses as reflected on this form of your wound meant?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody explained anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd now like to -- look at another document that also should not be broadcast to the public. And that's 1D946. And, sir, now we have this document on the screen, I'd ask you to take a moment to glance at it and let me know if you can confirm that this is the discharge sheet from the outpatient clinic of the Tuzla garrison of the Armija BiH relating to your discharge from their care?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is. It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at the first page where it has listed your military unit, there's listed OS and then the translator's note: Armed forces Srebrenica. Again I have to ask you: Does this accord with the information that you gave the medical care providers at the Tuzla garrison clinic?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't provide any information to anyone. I was supposed to be discharged, and they wrote this discharge sheets in the same way as they did for everybody else. They should also read the 2nd Corps because I was at the garrison infirmary, not at the Gradina Clinical Centre. So the Gradina Medical Centre was not the one who was supposed to issue this document, but, rather, the garrison infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm a little confused, sir. I believe looking at the B/C/S original of the form that it was the "ambulanta garizona Tuzla" that issued this form. Is that what you're talking about, that they were not supposed to issue the form?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They should have issued it because I was hospitalised at the garrison infirmary because all the beds were occupied in the Gradina Clinical Centre, and I was not the only one there. There were four rooms full of the wounded from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now this document is signed by a medical doctor. Do you recall this doctor as being one of the persons who treated you while you were at the infirmary of the Tuzla garrison?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. On the morning of the 17th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, on this version, the -- the -- we have again the diagnosis written in Latin that appears on the English and the B/C/S, and I want to ask you, sir: Did anyone at the garrison explain to you -- at the garrison infirmary explain to you that their diagnosis was that your wound was as a result of an explosion rather than a bullet?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was an entry/exit wound, and it can clearly be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about the diagnosis recorded by the medical staff that looked at you. Did they explain that their diagnosis as written implies an explosive injury not related to a bullet?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could see that the wound was called by -- caused by a gun-shot wound, not an explosion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness RM314, that's not answering the question. The question is: Did anybody at the clinic when you were discharged explain to you how, in their view, you got injured? Did anybody explain anything to you about your injury?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, a much better question. I'd like to tender this document also under seal, Your Honours, as the next exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number and be kept under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D946 receives number D283, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Registrar. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a question in relation to this document to the witness, please. We see that this is a form, the document is the a form, you would agree with that, used by the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the first line, we see first name, father's name, last name. This is printed. Then somebody has written your name. Behind that, we see "vojna jedinica." That seems to be "military unit" in the translation. This is also part of the printed form. Would you agree with that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is written military unit in the form. But they filled out this form. And they registered all of us as the wounded from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just want to make the distinction between the printed part of this document and the handwritten part. Behind the words military unit, in B/C/S of course, what can you read there in handwriting in the first line of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] OS Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you sure that this is OS or could it be JS or something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's OS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I put this question because in the English translation the translators were not sure about the letter O and put a question mark there, in the translation. At the bottom of this document, on the left side, you see something which is translated as: "Note: After being discharged from the medical institution, the patient should immediately report to the doctor attached to his military unit." This is part of the printed form; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did anyone in your -- in the clinic tell you what that means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to now move on to your 92 ter statement - again this should not be broadcast to the public - P1435, marked for identification. And we should be looking for page 3 in the English at the top of the page. Page 2 in the Bosnian at the very bottom of the page. And it leads onto the next page in the B/C/S. And, sir, the part I want to focus on is this time when you were discovered by the four men in police uniform. When you surrendered to them they asked you if you had a weapon. You said did you not. They looked in your bag and they found a hand-grenade that you had in there. And I want to ask you, sir: How did you happen to obtain a hand-grenade? Was it issued to you by the armed forces of the Armija BiH in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was given it by acquaintance of mine on the road between Srebrenica and Susnjari.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then I would like to focus on the next part of your testimony in this statement, which I believe is on the next page in the B/C/S. It's still on the same page in English. The next part you talk about in the next paragraph is an incident where you were walking and came across the body of a civilian that had blown himself up with a hand-grenade. And I want to ask you, sir: Was it a -- was it a common practice known to you that civilian males from Srebrenica were distributed hand-grenades?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. Nobody gave us any grenades. We just tried to solve this in any way we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now you say that you thought the individual had committed suicide based on what you observed. I want to look at another document with you, and this also should not be broadcast. It's 1D940. And this is again the statement that you gave in August 1995 to an investigating judge in Tuzla. And when we get that document, I think we'll need page 4 in both languages. And it's near the top, sir. There's the line, and I'll read it for you in English. It says: "At that moment a civilian ran out of the grass in front of me, threw down a hand-grenade on the edge of the asphalt road and killed himself with the blast without wounding a single Chetnik." Sir, is this part truthfully and accurately recounting what you told the investigating judge in Tuzla on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is -- is this the same incident you describe in your statement that we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so is it now your testimony that you actually eye-witnessed the individual running out of the grass and throwing the hand-grenade?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him throwing the hand-grenade. He was on a higher ground in respect of me. When they noticed me on the asphalt road, the policemen and soldiers in camouflage uniforms shot over our heads and shouting, Surrender. He was above me. And, in fear, he threw the grenade and killed himself. Later on, after I was captured and taken towards the school, they asked me if he was my brother, and whether I knew him. And then they ordered me to pull him by the legs onto the grass. He was lying on the asphalt road with his face down, and there was a lot of blood. In other words, I don't know the identity of that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to look at another document with you. And, again, this also should not be broadcast. And it is 1D944 in e-court. And if we can have the second page in both languages. Sir, this is a 2006 proofing session that you had with the Office of the Prosecutor. And I want to ask you about -- it's the last item on the second page in the English to see if this accords with what you just told us. And I will read it for you. It's actually going to be the next page in the B/C/S, I believe. Yes. There you go. It's the lasts item on the page in B/C/S now as well, sir. And it says there: "The witness also indicated that references in his prior statements to his having observed an individual commit suicide by detonating a grenade are incorrect in that no such direct observation was made." Does this report made by the Prosecution accord with what you told them and what you truthfully describe about this incident?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I didn't see him kill himself. I simply found him on the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the record, I don't think it's fair to put a contradiction to the witness as the witness just said what -- now confirm in his answers meaning that he didn't directly observe that. And that is what is recorded in the ICTY statement. So I think this corresponds to what we read now in the proofing note that the explosion, let's say, wasn't directly observed. So just ... it's fair [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... what's your objection, madam --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: That I think the witness is being presented with contradictions that are not actually true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Must a contradiction necessarily be true, Madam D'Ascoli?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I'm saying on the basis of what he just said, the follow-up question was not the contradiction the way was put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought the question was, Does this statement, this report accord to what you told the Prosecution. The answer to that is yes or no. And I think the witness answered the question. Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you in relation to the hand-grenade that you had on your possession, do you recall what type of hand-grenade it was and what type of prior experience you had had with such devices?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't see the man. I didn't see him kill himself. It was just that the hand-grenade detonated. The Serb soldiers and policemen were firing over our heads, shouting to surrender. I didn't even see the man close to me in the grass or -- until I saw him on the tarmac, dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps -- perhaps I misspoke or you did not understand my question. I was asking in relation to the hand-grenade that you had in your possession in your bag. What type was it, and what experience or instruction had you had prior --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you split the two questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What type was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What type was it, the hand-grenade in your bag?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a standard hand-grenade, which was not activated. It was in my bag that had been given to me by a man in order to have it at hand, should I fall into the Serb hands. As regards any previous experience, I served my term in the JNA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you, Witness. Please try to listen to the question. You're not being asked to explain how you acquired it. You're just being asked to explain what type it was. You said it is a standard hand-grenade. If that's the entirety of your explanation of what type it is, stop there. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say it was a standard hand-grenade. Was it a standard offensive or defensive hand-grenade, because I understand both are in the arsenal of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what type of hand-grenade it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At the time that you were given the hand-grenade by the acquaintance, were you given any instruction as to how to use it?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move on to ask you to return to the point in time when you were with the column of able-bodied men as you set out from Srebrenica when the Serbs were approaching.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you go there, Mr. Ivetic. I asked you to split your question, sir. You have not asked the second part of your question. You asked if he was given instructions when he acquired it and not asking what prior experience he has --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- of hand-grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I thought he already answered when he said he had used them in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what type of prior experience you had handling this particular type of hand-grenade?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was there any colour code on the grenade in question that you had in your possession?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was simply black.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'm having trouble understanding your last answer. Is that -- did you have prior experience handle this particular type of hand-grenade, is perhaps the better question.

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered a moment ago. I said no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, as I said I'd like to move back in time to the point when you were with the column of able-bodied men setting out from Srebrenica and you were -- I want to look at the Popovic transcript where in open session you talked about some items related to the 12- to 15.000 men that you mention in your 92 ter statement. If we can have 1D952 and page 63 in e-court at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is 952 to be publicised?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was in public session in Popovic so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And further I believe that the nature of the items will not identify this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I will read for you since we only have it English, as the transcripts are in English, and please follow along and I will ask you to first verify if this is all accurate and in accord with your recollection of your testimony and then some follow-up questions. Beginning at line 1: "Q. And approximately a third of those were armed. That was in your statement; correct? "A. In one part, yes. However, the exact information -- "Q. Those are your estimates. So according to your estimates, 4.000 to 5.000 armed soldiers were in the column towards Tuzla. Do you agree? "A. No. "Q. You would still agree the column was 12.000 to 15.000 and about a third of them were armed, from what you could see; correct? "A. I was talking about Buljim when I mentioned one-third, and as for the entire column and how many people went through the lines, you have to ask somebody else that. "Q. Well, I'm asking you, sir, because you're here and I'm going to ask you another question. In your statement, you indicated when the column started out that there were armed men, able-bodied men with arms, that were spread out between and amongst the people who were not armed; correct? "A. It was people returning to bring across people without weapons who did not manage to cross the first Serb lines at Buljim in the early morning. "Q. Now, did all of the people that you observed in that column who had arms, hunting rifles, pistols, grenades, whatever, were they all in camouflage uniforms or were some of them just dressed like civilians, like you? "A. No. Many of them were in civilian clothes." Now, sir, do you confirm and stand by this testimony from Popovic as being both truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by this testimony, and that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to move along to page 87 in e-court to present you with another portion of your prior testimony. And this time if we could focus on line 4. And again, sir, I will read it for you and ask you some questions relative to the same: "Q. Earlier you testified about Susnjari and about the number of people to be found in Susnjari. You said that since you mentioned that one-third of the men were armed among the able bodied people, you did not mention Susnjari but about Buljim when you testified in the Krstic case; is that right? "A. Yes. "Q. I'd like to read out this part of the testimony, your testimony in the Krstic case. "Ms. Faveau: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. President. "Q. You said page 3240 [In English] 'I went with all the other men towards the village of Slatina and Susnjari upwards.' And then the Prosecution [sic] asked you this: 'About how many other men were gathered in the area of Susnjari when you got there?' And you responded: 'Well, there were about 12 and 15. I can't give you an exact figure but there were a lot of us.' And then the question was: 'Do you know roughly how many of those men might have been armed in some way?' And your response was: 'As far as I was able to note, about a third, I would say, with hunting rifles, with not very strong weaponry, hunting rifles and other types but a third of them, I would say, not more.' "[Interpretation] Do you agree that in the Krstic case you did mention or you did speak about Susnjari and you were mentioning 12- to 15.000 people and a third of them were armed." And if question go on the next page: "A. Yes. "Q. Was your testimony accurate? "A. Yes. "Q. Was it also fair to say that when you arrived in Susnjari, somebody told you to line up so that civilians and military would be all mixed together? "A. All the men who arrive there were there. I don't know what you mean when you say ... military. All the men, irrespective of age, they were all there." Now, sir, do you stand by this selection of the Popovic transcript as being truthful and accurately depict what your testimony was, as you remember it?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is truthful and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I'd like to look at one other selection about the column and that's in 1D949, which also is a public session transcript, and I don't believe it will identify the witness. And we're looking at page 7 in e-court which should correlate to transcript page 2341 of the Krstic trial. And if we could look at line 3 onwards, sir. And again I will read so you get translation of what the transcript says and then I'll ask you the same questions as with the other selections: "Q. Was that the evening of the 11th or was it noon on the 12th? "A. It was in the evening of the 12th -- no, I'm sorry. It was between the 11th and 12th. We started out on the 11th, at about 2.30, and in the evening we arrived at Susnjari at about 10.00. We had a consultation there. So that at about 12.00 midnight, that is to say we started out, the night between the 11th and the 12th. "Q. What was this consultation you referred to? "A. Well, we lined up so that as many people could cross as possible, because the Serb lines were very near and there were a lot of us. Around Csusi and the surrounding hills, that's where they were. "Q. Was someone leading the consultation or leading this large group of men? "A. No. They just tried to line us up so that people with weapons and without weapons would be mixed up together, and if we came across an ambush, to prevent as many people losing their lives as possible." And, sir, now having listened to this selection of your testimony from Krstic, do you stand by the same as being truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is truthful and accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now at this time, Your Honours, I think I do need to go into private session to discuss one topic that may lead to the witness being identified if it's in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And straight into closed session again. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Thank you. I do have some re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, well, I just have a few additional questions that I want to ask to clarify the record. While I know that after you testified three times already before the Tribunal it is very difficult for you to be here and to go through all your evidence, right? So I'll try to -- I understand that and so please bear with me. I'll try to be brief. Now, yesterday my colleague Mr. Ivetic spent quite some time yesterday and today discussing some of your prior statements. One of these statements that Mr. Ivetic showed to you yesterday was a handwritten statement, your handwriting, dated the 31st of July, 1995, and written at the Tuzla garrison infirmary. This was admitted as Exhibit D00281. This was discussed yesterday at transcript pages 10877 to 10882. You might remember also Judge Fluegge asked you some questions and clarifications about it. Now, I believe there was some confusion about which statement that was what you believed that was, so I'll try to clarify that so please bear with me. We researched the provenance of this handwritten statement and we saw we received it from the ABiH 2nd Corps headquarters in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So I want to call up 65 ter 28893 and if I can please have the first page of both the English and the B/C/S on e-court. Your Honours, this is a newly up loaded documents that was not on our 65 ter exhibit list. It is a daily report of the ABiH 2nd Medical Battalion of the 2nd Corps with attached handwritten statement dated 31st of July, 1995. There is the same handwritten statement that we -- you know, I discuss was admitted as D281. This document was disclosed in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Should not be broadcast, I think. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: That first page, yes, not to be broadcast. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've given quite a lot of evidence. Can we get to re-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... no objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection to the use of the document. It was the first page I was missing in e-court yesterday, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't see it yesterday so I'm showing it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So if we read -- if we -- well, if we read the date we see that it is dated the 31st of July and the reporting issue is unauthorised remarks or statements given to the media. Now, sir, do you see the document on the screen? And can you read the paragraph after the -- after it says "reporting issue"? Now we read that, "Due to a failure on the part of the staff at the reception of the Tuzla garrison infirmary to carry out their tasks properly, persons who were not identified," according to your written statement, took a statement from you, from the witness. And then, okay, we have the signature, the -- the security commander -- reporting commander also says that statements will be taken by Nurse Rasema, and the person at the reception that you mention in your statement. Now yesterday in answering one of the questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yesterday, in response to a question by Judge Fluegge, you said that you didn't have an intention of giving a statement whatsoever. I was rather forced by those who were securing the infirmary to make this statement. This is line -- well, this is it page 10882 lines 3 to 5. And then when asked -- when you were asked to explain what you mean by "they," you said that -- yeah, they introduced themselves as security officer of the infirmary. So, now, my question is, because we see that this document, which, you know, like is a daily report attached to your statement and your statement of the same date, the 31st of July, while in your statement, in your handwritten statement attached to this document, you discuss, you explain what happened on the 27th of July, when unidentified person together working with journalists came and asked you to give a statement, so were you trying to say or is it your testimony that -- well, sorry. Let me put it this way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think you must ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't testify.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So is this statement the handwritten statement attached to this document, the one dated 31st of July, is that the statement you gave to the security officers of the infirmary to explained what happened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking if it's two different statements that we're discussing. One --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: One question at a time.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So, sir, maybe if we can go to the second page of this document so that the handwritten statement appears on the -- on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. Go how you want to go, but please ask questions, Madam D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, is this handwritten statement the statement that you gave to the security officer of the infirmary to explain what happened some days before?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I had to give this statement under duress, despite my wishes. And this statement is incomplete. It is true that it was given to the men who provided the previous document, in which it says that it is incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Witness, my question is: Are we talking about two different events and two different statements: This one that you gave to the officers of the infirmary, because they -- to explain what happened; and a separate one that you referred to in this statement, that was the one that the -- the unidentified person and the journalists asked from you. Are we talking about two different statements?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The second statement signed by the 2nd Corps was not the one I gave. This one I gave under duress, and it's inconsistent with that, but since I was in the garrison infirmary, he came to see me and said, You must give a statement to me because I'm a security officer here who must obtain information. So this is my statement. And I think it's one and the same statement; only he inserted a reservation there that it was incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: When you said this is not consistent with the -- with the previous one, you mean with the statement that you gave to the journalist?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement that is on the screen now was not the one I gave to the journalist but, rather, to Smajo Elezovic, a security officer at the infirmary. And one can see that the previous document was signed by Major Elezovic. Only the paper that is handwritten is the one that I provided.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I would add this document -- I would tender this document into evidence. I don't think there's a way of adding it to the previous one so I would just tender it as a separate Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] sorry. Is this document 28893. That's what you called earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's a correct 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. 28893 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May it please be admitted into evidence and given a number under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28893 receives number P1441, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Under seal. Now, Witness, when you say you wrote this statement under duress, did the person or persons who were forcing you, tell you what to write?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no. They gave me a piece of paper and told me to write a statement about what I had lived through. I started writing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You answered my question. Thank you so much. Yes, madam, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, during cross-examination yesterday, you refer a number of times to your mental psychological state after the execution you survived and while you were at the infirmary in Tuzla. Can you tell us for how long overall you were in the infirmary for your wound and how long did it take you to recover physically and to fell better emotionally?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I think that I stayed at the garrison infirmary about two and a half weeks. After that, I was discharged, but I had to go to the closest local clinic to have my wound bandaged. We were all displaced, and I have to say that after everything that I went through, the situation is not improving. I am still feeling more and more ...

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Do you want to complete the answer? I just see, "I am still feeling more and more ..."

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, both physically and mentally. I need to undergo a surgery. But what can I tell you? For as long as I can sustain as it is now, I will try to move on and -- with my life.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I understand, sir. Can you tell us how the situation was like when you arrived at the Tuzla infirmary? Were there many wounded? Was the situation -- how was the situation like.

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was chaotic. The wounded were arriving virtually every minute. The Gradina Medical Centre was overbooked. We couldn't be admitted there, so they moved us to the infirmary where the doctors provided medical assistance to us, and documents can confirm that it was the BH Army who did it. So what else can I say? Everything was chaotic. Nobody knew exactly what to do. They used all these forms to provide discharge sheets. There was a lot of discussion about that, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: When they took care of you and of your wound, did you tell the doctors or whomever assisted you, the date when you were wounded?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I told them the date when I was wounded. When I received the first proper care at Gradina, I remember the surgeon shouting at me and asking me, Why did you wait so long? I just felt that he was making incisions around the bones because the wound was already old, and that's all that I can remember. I remember that at 10.00 I was taken to the garrison infirmary and that if I needed another surgery the next day they would send me back to Gradina. I stayed there for a week bedridden, and, after that, I had to use crutches.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So you said you told them about the day. Which is what -- what did you tell them? When your -- when you were wounded, which day you -- did you tell them that happened.

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told them that on the second day after the breakthrough, I was captured on the morning of the 13th, and that in the afternoon of that same day, I was shot, and that on the 13th I was alone in the forest, and that on the 14th, I headed off towards Goldric [phoen] and I described my trip.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. And as you testified also yesterday, I think you said the executions by the Jadar river happened some time between 10.00 or 11.00, before 12 -- 12.00 in the morning of the 13th; correct?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, my colleague Mr. Ivetic also spent quite some time going through your prior statements and transcripts and discussing different issues from both statements and transcripts. Now, out of those discussed yesterday, there are two inaccuracies related to -- brought to your attention yesterday and related to your ICTY statement of 16 August 1995 now marked with -- as P1435. So I want to recapitulate these inconsistencies, you know, to make -- just to have a clean record. The first one was your occupation, well, current occupation back in 1995 which was recorded on the front page of the ICTY statement as member of the Bosnian army, soldier, and yesterday you said this was incorrect. So this was the first one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam D'Ascoli, I have a concern that your prefix to your questions are just so long.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You could just asked this witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In one of your statements this is what they say your job is. Can you explain that. Okay? Just ask him to explain the job, member of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Well, I think the witness explained the job, so my question was a different one. I was just recapitulating for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Put the question. Put a different question.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So, sir, now, besides these two inaccuracies in your ICTY statement, can you tell us if these are so fundamental to impact the substance and the core parts of your evidence about events at Konjevic Polje and the shooting at the Jadar river of which you are a survivor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think that is asking for a legal conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I still don't know what counsel is asking: Besides these --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- two inaccuracies in your statement and the core part of your evidence about events at Konjevic Polje and the shooting at the Jadar river, I'm not sure what -- This has nothing to do with the job --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Your Honours, I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- title as explained on the statement, which I thought is what you were going to ask about.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honour, my question was whether besides those two inaccuracies which was our -- which I was recapitulating for the record, but then I'm skipping that part, besides, you know, and considering those two inaccuracies, if the substance of the statement in relation to the events at Konjevic Polje, the execution on the Jadar river which he survived, if that fundamental part is correct. And if you stand by that, by the evidence in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Re-examination is not for reasserting what you have said but for clarifying any things that need clarification. We know that. One, you don't have to recapitulate. We've got it on the record. You're duplicating the record. Two, he has not being cross-examined on the substance of events that took place, and therefore there is no need for you to ask him whether he stands by that. But, anyway, carry on, Madam D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Well, my question was whether the witness stands by the truthfulness and accuracy of the evidence that you, sir, provided in your ICTY statements. After I get an answer, then I rest my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ask for the answer, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, do you stand by the truthfulness of the evidence provided in your ICTY statements, the three that we discussed yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RM314 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I stand by those statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: That concludes my re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. RM314, that brings us to the end of your testimony. The Chamber would like to thank you very much for coming to testify. We understand that you've testified in a number of cases and you probably are getting tired of coming here. We appreciate that once again you've come. We wish you a safe trip back home. You may now stand down. You are excused from further attending. May the Chamber please move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. There's still the issue of the three MFI statement of the witness. P1435, 1436, and 1437. I would ask them to be admitted into evidence, considering -- after, you know, the witness was cross-examined on those statements by the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we made our submissions in writing and orally yesterday. I don't need to burden you with repeating them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The three statements 1435, 6, and 7 are admitted, and then marked for identification. Status may be removed. May they be kept under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Anything else, Madam D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Thank you. If I may be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Hochhauser, are you ready to call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm told we need to go into closed session again for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we please go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. Good afternoon, Witness RM297. You have asked for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- protective measures. I wanted to just remind you that because of the protective measures you asked for we're not going to call you by your name. We're going to call you by your pseudonym. We will be calling you RM297. The other protective measures that you have is that of face distortion so your face will not be seen by people outside this courtroom. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you then please make the declaration to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else. And please stand up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may now be seated. You will now be examined by Madam Hochhauser who is the representative for the Prosecution. She is to your right. Madam Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness RM297. As the Chamber has just informed you that will be how we refer to you in this courtroom. If we could have 65 ter number 28879 on the monitor, please, not to be broadcast. And, Witness, when you are able to see what's on the monitor in front of you, can you confirm for the Chamber whether that accurately records your name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's admitted into evidence. 28879 under seal, may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28879 receives number P1442, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And you have also given statements to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal on several occasions, including statements dated 20 August 1996, 14 June 2001, and 13 and 14 August 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: If we could please have 65 ter 28878 on the monitor, also not to be broadcast outside of the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, as this is coming up on the monitor, I'll ask you whether yesterday you had an opportunity to review the statement dated 13 to 14 August 1995?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And now --

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, looking at the monitor, do you recognise that to be that -- what's showing on the monitor now, to be that statement?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now yesterday in reviewing this statement, you noticed that in the B/C/S translation, there were two translation errors which you corrected. First, at page 2, paragraph 2 --

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: -- of B/C/S -- I'm just going complete the question before -- I know that you suspect already what I'm going to ask you, but if you can let me put the full question to you. First at page 2 paragraph 2 in the B/C/S where it gives the date for the fall of Srebrenica, it should read "11 July" not "1 July"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And, secondly, on page 3 of the B/C/S, in the last sentence of the third paragraph on the page, the sentence referring to General Mladic, it should read "after he finished his speech, the prisoners said thank you, commander," where it now reads in the translation "his soldiers," instead of "prisoners"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] of those were correct in the English. So also in your statement -- in this statement, at page 3 in the English and B/C/S -- in both English and B/C/S, you talk about your brother whose first name appears in the statement, and you describe that you were separated from him in the Sandici meadow when you were ordered onto trucks and have not had news of him since. Now without saying his name because it is written in the statement, can you tell the Chamber if you've had any more recent information on your brother than the time that you made this statement?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Well, yes. They say that they found some of his bones but the mortal remains are not complete.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: But you were informed that -- that some of his remains were identified; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, other than -- well, and actually -- again without saying your brother's name, the first name of which appears in the statement, does he share the last -- the same last name as you do?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, other than these two translation corrections and the additional piece of information that we've just discussed, are there any other changes or corrections that you would make to the statement after having reviewed it?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: So if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked when you gave that statement back in 1995, would you provide the same information?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: I think I would provide the same information.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. In substance, even if not the exact same language, the same substantive information.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Well, one cannot repeat each and every word.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. But the substance of what you would say, it would be the same; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And is the information in that statement both truthful and accurate, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: It definitely is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to move closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Witness, I don't know if you can hear the note, but the interpreters are asking you to move your chair a little bit closer to the microphone. They're having a little bit of trouble hearing you. Closer. Closer to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Court Usher, can you help the witness there to make sure he gets closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Your Honours, at this point I would tender 65 ter 28878 into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 28878 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28878 receives number P1443, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Yes, Madam Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the Court's permission, I would like to read a summary of the witness's evidence for the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may go ahead, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: On 14th March of 1993 after being forced from him home municipality, RM297 and his two brothers moved to the protected enclave of Srebrenica where they remained until the fall of that enclave on 11 July 1995. On that date, the witness and one of his brothers decided to join the other able-bodied men in escaping through the woods. They assembled with thousands of other Muslim men in the nearby village of Susnjari, which if I've mispronounced is S-u-s-n-j-a-r-i. On 12 July, the witness and this -- and this group of Muslim men set off in a long column. The witness split off from the main column with a group of about a thousand men who were mostly civilians, a few soldiers, and some wounded. As they were in the woods, Bosnian Serb soldiers called to the Muslim men to surrender and promised that if they did, they would stay alive. After one night in the woods, the witness and the men he was with surrendered in a meadow to a group of soldiers wearing the insignia of the Army of Republika Srpska. They were held in that meadow where in the afternoon General Mladic came and addressed the witness and other prisoners, promising them that they would be exchanged. Later that same evening, the prisoners were boarded onto buses and trucks and were taken to Bratunac. The witness spent that night, 13 into 14 July, inside of a truck parked outside of the Vihor garages. During the night, soldiers shouted out for prisoners from certain villages, and those who answered were taken off the trucks. RM297 could hear the sounds of beating, screams, shots being fired, and those prisoners were not seen by him again. The next day, 14 July, the trucks and buses left Bratunac in a long convoy of vehicles, and the witness was brought with the other men to the elementary school in Orahovac. The witness estimates that when people stopped filing in, the gym held approximately 1.000 men and the prisoners were all packed together tightly against each other. When one prisoner yelled out that they should not be killed, that prisoner was taken out of the hall. The witness heard shots and screams and that prisoner was never seen again. The men were eventually brought row by row to the exit of the gymnasium where they were each given a glass of water and blindfolded. Once blindfolded, the prisoners were told they were being taken to a camp in Bijeljina and they were loaded onto trucks. Instead the trucks drove the short distance to a field in Orahovac and the witness, along with the other men he was with were told to get off the truck. The witness and the men he was with were lined up in rows and shot at. The witness managed to survive these executions by feigning death as he lay under the body of another victim. As he lay underneath and amongst the dead bodies, RM297 could hear that approximately every 10 to 15 minutes, a new truck full of prisoners would arrive, and those prisoners were executed, were killed, in the same manner. The witness could hear that this continued for hours. After night-fall, as the witness lay still underneath -- still underneath the dead bodies, he heard some of the executioners speaking to one another and he recognised the first name and the distinctive voice of Gojko Simic, a man that RM297 had known for years. Later that night when the soldiers were distracted, RM297 was able to escape into the woods. As he ran away he got turned around at one point and found himself back at the killing site and saw that the field was covered in bodies. After several very difficult days of moving and hiding, RM297 managed to reach safety in Muslim held territory. And, Your Honours thank you for your patience with the length of that summary. That concludes it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And if I may, I have a few questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, Witness RM297, as you know the Judges have already read your statement and are very familiar with the information you put in it, so I'm only going to ask you a few additional questions. First, can you please tell the Judges why was it that you decided to leave Srebrenica on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: We decided to do that as we knew what was going to happen with Srebrenica. Srebrenica was not the only one. There were several such locations. It's just that never else were 8- to 9.000 people killed in a few days. There was Visegrad, Vojnica, Foca, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc and elsewhere. The people there had a very similar experience to ours. It's just that such a large-scale genocide did not take place anywhere else other than Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sir, when you say "we knew," can you just tell us what it is that you -- that you anticipated, what you feared was going to happen that made you leave? And can I also ask you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Well, you know, Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic are friends. And before Srebrenica fell, they said they would take revenge on Srebrenica. The very fact that Ratko Mladic arrived there confirms that. He called Srebrenica Srpska, Serbian Srebrenica, and he promised to take revenge on the Turks and the janissaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you some specific questions directed at specific parts of your testimony -- of your statement, okay? Can you -- on your -- excuse me. In the statement which is now in evidence as P1443 -- yes, as P1443, on page 4, in both languages, in the third paragraph, you talk about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have it on the screen, please, Madam Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Under seal. It should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Under seal. Thank you. And it would be page 4 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And as it's coming up, Witness I know this feels like jumping around in -- in the statement and in -- in the whole story of what happened to you, but if you can just try to focus on specifically what I'm drawing your attention to, okay? In page 4 in -- it's in the third paragraph in the English and it's slightly lower down in the B/C/S, you discuss seeing a -- a United Nations APC while you and the other men were being driven to the gymnasium. Can you tell the Chamber whether you ever saw that APC again later and what were the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: As we were going from the quarry in Zvornik to Divic, the people saw that an APC, an UN APC, was also part of the column. When we arrived in Orahovac in the courtyard, they parked to the left. There were two uniformed soldiers in UNPROFOR uniforms with automatic rifles. Their rifles were not UNPROFOR rifles, though. On the APC, it no longer read UNPROFOR but the letter C. In the Cyrillic script, it is S. There was a 50-year-old man in civilian clothes probably trying to pass off as an interpreter. They did not address us. We were ordered to get off the trucks and to run to the school building. I had a leather jacket on. The person standing some way away instructed us to leave our clothes on a pile and he told me to leave my jacket there as well. All of my documents were in it. We barged into the hallway and we turned left after some 5 to 6 metres. When we entered the hall it was already half full or more than half.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Hochhauser, try to control your witness. Witness, can we just try to answer the question that was put to you. You were asked: Did you ever see that APC after that day. Can you give us that first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. That's what you asked, Madam Hochhauser, so you can't ask the next part of your question. There would be no circumstances of seeing it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sir, the APC in -- in the statement, you describe seeing it on the road. Did you see it again at the gymnasium, that's the second time that you saw it, when you describe it was then painted with Cyrillic lettering on it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who is testifying, Madam Hochhauser?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Judge, Your Honour, I'm not trying to testify. I'm trying to clarify what the witness said because he did address a second time and I understood from your question that that might not have been clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you now several questions about your treatment during the whole time-period that you were detained. So from the meadow until you made your escape from the pit in Orahovac, okay? So that's the time-period that I'm addressing. Did you, during that time-period, ever see or hear any of the Serb soldiers take names or write lists of names at any point during this time period?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time, Madam Hochhauser, to take a break?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes, it would be fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May the Chamber please move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Before you continue, Madam Hochhauser, I've got one little point to raise here with the Defence. Mr. Lukic, Mr. Groome said this morning - and it was in closed session unfortunately - there are -- said something about Witness Riedlmayer, and what the Chamber would like to know is do you still need the 30-day extension of time starting from today, when is the day you are now being provided with the translation, or are you comfortable to meet the deadline?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thirty days from today, Your Honour. Thirty days from today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then 30 days from today we give you. The deadline is then set at 10 June.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome. Madam Hochhauser, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we can please have the statement, P1443, back up on the monitor, not to be broadcast. And it's at page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: In what is the second -- sorry, I would describe it as the second full paragraph in the English, and the first large -- large paragraph in the B/C/S version. You describe in that portion of your statement being in the meadow and Mr. Mladic arriving. And it says there: "He promised us we would get some water."

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Did you receive any water after that?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Well, yes. We had been receiving water before Mladic's arrival. But he told us that we would be going to the hangars, that we would not be given any supper, only water.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And after seeing him -- after that exchange with -- excuse me. After being addressed by Mr. Mladic when you were brought to the gymnasium, were you given any food or water?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: No. Well, we did receive water but not enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, and I'm referring to the entire time of your detention, from the time -- from the meadow when you first surrendered yourself until the -- the execution field, so that whole period. Can you tell -- can you describe, please, how the Serb soldiers spoke to you and the other prisoners? What kind of language was used?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: They only swore at our Turkish and Balija mothers. Otherwise, they did not insult us in any other way. The soldier who had a black scarf, he said to every group that arrived, that the governments were in negotiations and that there will be an exchange, all for all.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And when you say "they only swore at our Turkish and Balija mothers," was that -- can you describe the circumstances of that?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Well, of course, they swore at our Turkish and Balija mothers, saying that this was the Serbian land, and that the Serbian army was invincible. We were forced to keep silent, but we know very well how difficult it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Turning specifically to the time-period of the executions in the field, can you tell us if you heard any exchanges between wounded men and the Serb soldiers who had been shooting them; and, if so, what was said, what you heard?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: There was a seriously injured man. He asked to be finished off. Only God knows how he felt. One of the Serb soldiers, because, of course, all of us were lying prostrate on the ground, the -- he just said, Slowly, slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: When you say "he said, Slowly, slowly," who said? The wounded person or someone else?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: One of the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: If we could please have on the monitor, P1132, which is the book of photographs, maps and aerials used with Witness Jean-Rene Ruez. And if we could begin at page 129 in e-court, and I don't know if anybody else has available to them the hard copy of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not in court here, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. So then page 129 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Witness, can you -- Witness, in June of 1999, did you accompany Investigator Ruez from the OTP to certain sites described in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now I'll ask you to look at what is now on the monitor. And if we could please show --

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes. That's the school. In this narrow part --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not going to ask you to mark anything on it. If you can put down the pen for one second.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask, please, if we can display page 129 and then flip to 130, through 133, so the witness has an opportunity to see each of those photographs, in turn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I need to show you something?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I'm going ask you as you look at these to tell us whether those are locations that you went to with Investigator Ruez.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And are those the locations that you pointed out as having been described in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, if we could please turn to page 134 of this exhibit in e-court. Can you tell us what it is that we're looking at in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Well, these are the bullet-holes fired by the soldiers who were standing at the door.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: All right. And what were the circumstances in which those shots were being fired?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Well, there was a commotion among the people, it was very hot, there was not enough air, and they fired these warning shots from the door.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: If we could please turn to page 142 and 143 in e-court. And, Witness, can you tell us if you recognise this location -- the location that's shown on pages 142 and 143 of Exhibit P1132?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And from where?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Because when I escaped, I ran across the railway track. Because when we first arrived, I didn't know the place where we came.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And did you point out those locations to Investigator Ruez as -- as the field that you had been in?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, if we could move briefly into private session for a series of questions that might have some personal detail in the answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Registrar. When you are ready, you may start, Mr. Lukic. Witness 297, you're now going to be examined by Defence counsel, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We are hearing a buzzing sound in our earphones. Can something be done about it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if you can help. Witness, did you -- can you hear the lawyer in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He said to you good afternoon. I didn't hear you answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said good afternoon. But maybe not loud enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, both of us speak the same or similar language, so kindly wait for a while after my question and I will wait a while after your answer so that everything can be recorded. Let me start with the period quite before the events that are the core of your testimony, and gradually we'll come to that. You used to be a member of the armed forces after the start of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, both your bothers were alive.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, I had three brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One of your brothers was killed in 1992.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your brothers were also members of the Territorial Defence in your native town. I'm not going to mention the name.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you and your brothers at that time served any call-up papers to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: No. But, Mr. Lukic, there was no JNA at the time. JNA was extinguished in the early 1990s. Immediately after the separation of, first, Croatia and Slovenia, and then Macedonia and Bosnia, the JNA ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did other people receive call-up papers in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The units that you belonged to after the beginning of the war were not under JNA command.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, just like all other members of your nation, a kind of mistrust towards the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Well, of course. We could have been the JNA only during the period of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia when everybody respected one single constitution and one single law, regardless of whether it was Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Kosovo, Vojvodina, et cetera. We had one single army and we trusted it, but this unfortunate army of ours was the one who killed us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
