utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to ask you to slow down. I can hear the interpreter rushing very much trying to keep a pace with you. So if you could slow down when you answer questions, please. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You felt mistrust towards the Serbs as well at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: No. We conducted negotiations with our Serb neighbours. We make agreement that, let's say, tonight a Serb will keep guard and then the Muslim would come to replace him. However, when the Muslim comes, the Serb was not there, and that is the reason why we lost our trust in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in that period there was a disruption in interethnic relations in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Well, of course. There would not have been any disruption of that kind had it not been for this Serbia of yours and that army which you prefer to call the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your area, did you receive any instructions from the Muslim political leadership not to join the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we please have 1D958 in e-court. I'm going to show you your testimony in the Karadzic case in order to refresh your memory about what you said on that occasion. I need page 25 in e-court, and then we'll move to the next page, which is 1363, transcript page lines 24 and 25, and then the first two lines on the next page. I'm going to read in English so that can you receive an interpretation: [In English] "Q. The question was whether Muslim soldiers and officers were leaving the JNA pursuant to instructions of your leadership and did your leadership prevent the response to the call-up."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're trying to find this. I'm not finding it, Mr. Lukic. If you can tell us again the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Line 24. And it starts ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Line 24 on this page says something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Twenty-five, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: The transcripts read -- transcript reads that you were calling our attention to page 1363 of the original transcript. That is not what is actually being shown on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can I see the top of the page, please. Then we have to move 30 pages ahead. If this is page 25, then we need 55. Now we can see. I -- thank you. Now we can see at line 24 the question was: "Whether Muslim soldiers and officers were leaving the JNA pursuant to instructions of your leadership, and did your leadership prevent the response to the call-up?" Answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If we can get the page turned over, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Answer, line 3: "A. Yes, it did." [Interpretation] Does it refresh your memory that you actually confirmed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The speakers overlapped. Could Mr. Lukic repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the interpreters ask that you repeat your question because you are overlapping. You're speaking all at the same time. Can you please wait for each other to finish what one is saying before the other answers. Repeat your question Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Kindly wait for me to conclude my question. Is it correct, therefore --

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Wait, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, please wait for Mr. Lukic to finish his question before you answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And make a pause, please, because the interpreters need the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So let's try again. Is it correct that your leadership provided instructions to the effect that people should not respond to JNA call-ups?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive instructions from the same leadership to join Muslim armed formations?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Well, to tell you directly, in our small towns and places where we were, we did not have such instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of something like that in the media?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Well, of course, everyone tried to protect themselves. Bosnia-Herzegovina is the only state in the world that was attacked and that did not have an arm force and yet it was attacked by this strong, unfortunate JNA, which carried out an aggression with our own weapons against us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You went one way, and your family the other, to Tuzla; correct?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you were withdrawing with your unit to another position.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: No. We did not withdraw with our unit. We were withdrawing because we were being driven away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Later, you arrived in the area of Konjevic Polje; correct?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the territory that you reached in Konjevic Polje, there were no Serbs left who had lived before -- who had lived there before?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: In Konjevic Polje, there were no Serbs. There were no Serbs in Konjevic Polje but there is a church constructed on Muslim land. I think it must be the only place in the world where there are no people who worship a particular religion and yet their church is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony today that your forces controlled the territory in which, before that, there had not been a single Serb village?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: No, no. There were Serb villages there. But in Konjevic Polje itself, there were no Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did the Serbs from the villages where they lived before leave? How did they come to leave?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: It's well known how they left. They attacked us from all sides and we had to -- well, because we were attacked from three sides, and we moved them. They went away. I don't know where to. Whereas, the other two sides remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say that you moved them, you mean you drove them away?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Well, it may seem like that but we didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I'm just going to start objecting to the general nature of these questions that are directed to sort of general -- generalised events in the conflict, as opposed to this witness's personal experience and knowledge during that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that this witness does have this experience and he is testify about his personal knowledge. He tells us when something in general he is not informed about. But I can even rephrase the question and ask him more specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead. Okay. Carry on, Mr. Lukic, and please stay relevant to the issues before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many Serbs were killed in the area controlled by your forces after your arrival?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the Serbs left the area, you are familiar with a case in which Slobodan Stojanovic, a boy of 11, was killed.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: As for the child, I am sorry for it because it was not to blame, but the rest of the Serbs were, in particular, his father and where the other Serbs were. They did not want to send their children, but they sent that one child so that they would not lose their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we please see 1D961 in e-court. In the Karadzic case, you were shown this photograph. Do you recognise the boy?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes, this is the child.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will just tender this into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm advised, Mr. Lukic, that there is an attachment with writings attached to this photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is a text newspaper's text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, so if you're tendering the photo maybe you must tender it separately, upload it separately, because we tender the photo only and not what is attached to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The gentleman confirmed what is in the text, in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. Not before us. Where? Where did he confirm that? He's just confirmed this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That he knows about the killing of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, no. He knows about this chart. And that's what you are tendering. That's what we have seen. We haven't seen any text.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can we see the text of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, go ahead. Why are we being shown a newspaper article now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness testified about his knowledge about the fate of this child. Isn't it -- that sufficient? Why do we need a newspaper article? This has no -- not a specific relevance for our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will ask additional question and maybe it will be clear then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, did you know that the boy was killed by a woman, Elfete Veseli, a member of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: That's what I heard. But, Mr. Lukic, if only one child were -- Muslim child were killed like this, it would have been much better. One must admit that he was a victim too, but when Bosniak children were being killed none of you from Serbia put any captions saying, One executioner or four one victim. What about the 200.000? What words should be used for 200.000? 100, 600 children were killed in Sarajevo alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, Witness, Witness can I ask you to please listen to the question carefully and just answer the question that is put to you. It is understandable that you might want to tell your story, but, you know, we -- your story has been told elsewhere, but here we would like to get answers to the questions that are put to you. We have very limited time. I asked you to please listen carefully and just answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And not say more. Yes, Mr. Lukic, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if the witness is going on, please stop him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you heard the Court's instructions. In future, I will have to cut you off if you expand too much.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: You cut me off? I have the right to say it. And the Judge has the right to cut me off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, okay, okay. I'll do it then. You go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who are you to cut me off? Only the Judges can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in Konjevic Polje -- well, you say that no Serbs lived there, but I'll give you this example. The father of General Simic lived there. General Simic was the commander of the East Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: I don't know that. What I do know is that some 30 years ago there were only two houses on the right side coming from Drinjaca to the town and there were two Serb houses there. I think they sold them and left. I don't think there was a single Serb there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As one enters Konjevic Polje and the area there, one does not find a single Serb there.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: I'm telling you that there were no Serbs. Perhaps in Paljevici only or in Drinjaca but not in Konjevic Polje. As far as I recall, that was so. I did not reside there, but I don't think there was a single Serb house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So from there, you went to Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, how many weapons were there in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Whatever weapons we had, we handed them over. Some may have had; some others didn't. Unless people kept it hidden. I guess UNPROFOR would know how many pieces of weapons there were. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have D270 in e-court. You know who Ramiz Becirovic was?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: I didn't know him personally. I was from another municipality, and he was from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that at the time he was Chief of Staff of the 28th Division of the land forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: It wasn't called division at the time. It was established only once Srebrenica fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have a document dated the 11th of August, 1995, before us. This is page 1. This statement was taken from Mr. Becirovic. We need page 4 in the B/C/S in e-court, and page 5 in the English version. Please look at the paragraph beginning with, "Once UNPROFOR arrived." Actually, no, the one after that: "After we got those two agreements on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica, we had to disarm completely. We barely managed to secure some older weapons in disrepair to hand over to UNPROFOR while the troops hid the rest at their homes. It was a custom for the troops to keep their weapons at their homes and only exceptionally were they handed out to other troops at the line. It was never permitted to have weapons grouped in one place." Would you allow for the possibility that Mr. Becirovic was better informed than you were in terms of what was going on with the weapons in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Well, if Mr. Becirovic was in that position, of course, he knew. I didn't know. I was just a fly on the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You never went to the confrontation line, or did you?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: No. I never went. I did stand guard, but I never took part in any operation or clash.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in Konjevic Polje some drivers from the Glinica company were killed?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Well, this is the first I hear it, from you. I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like you now to focus on the period when you and other men assembled in Susnjari. When you set off, you were at the rear of the column; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since you were at the rear, and you were walking behind the others, can you remember how many dead bodies you saw?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Immediately as we set off, there were five or six victims by a stream. I don't know who had killed them. And then, later on, when we came to a hill, there were at least dead bodies there -- 50 dead bodies there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that during your journey you saw around 500 dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D956 in e-court, please. We need page 844 of the transcript, which corresponds to page 13 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was in private session, at least the top of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have to go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I read lines from 10 to 12.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Yes, Mr. Lukic, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then we have to move to next page, 844, from the transcript. We need lines -- from lines -- from number 20, further on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, that's now in private session, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So may the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. That's right, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While the column was on the move from Susnjari towards Tuzla, did you notice that some people turned and went back towards Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: I didn't see them myself, but I did hear that some people returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Alongside you in the column were some people in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes, there were a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the fighting that was going on during the moving of the column?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Probably in this pile of 50 dead bodies we knew nothing about that. We, who were in the rear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You decided to surrender, and you went out onto the road where you were met by the Serb soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As soon as you appeared, they asked you -- you to give them money.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have a feeling then that they are being involved in some criminal activities?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Well, they were involved in crime throughout the war. They never did any -- any honest thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you surrendered, where were you in the column? Were you still in the rear? Were you in the middle? Or at the head?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I think I was somewhere in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After a while, the people who were guarding you rotated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what were you told about these newcomers?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: When the rotation came, the man with the black scarf said, These are Arkan's Men. I didn't see any specific insignia. I only noticed that they wore new camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After you were taken prisoner, you were -- you were taken to a meadow in Sandici and that is where you were told to sit down on the ground; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were sitting in rows about 20 metres long; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, maybe less, maybe more. I wasn't able to assess this exactly. If I had known that things will come to this, I would have tried to remember them better.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's all right. This is a rough estimate, and thank you for that. So, at the end of the day, when all the people gathered together, can you tell us how many rows were there?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Well there were many of them. I cannot tell you now how many rows there were, but there were quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's all right. If you can't do it, fine. There were some women and -- and -- young women with you when you surrendered; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They were allowed to board the buses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There were also boys under the age of 15 with you as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And they were also allowed to leave.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Well, when they released woman and the child of about 10 years of ages and two young girls, one of them who was the prettier one, the soldiers shouted at the one with the black scarf, Leave her, we might need her. But he kept quiet, didn't make any comment and said, There's a bus down there. And he told some boys to join them. Some dozen boys who were maybe of my height but very young went down there. There was one of them to was very tall, but he was told that he should sit down because he was capable of carrying a machine-gun, and after that, he did not let anyone else go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It hasn't been recorded as some dozen young boys were allowed to board the buses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that at one point, General Mladic appeared.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were told by someone who was with you, because you personally didn't recognise him.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: When Ratko Mladic and a group of officers or ordinary soldiers came with him, the people in the rows started shouting, Here comes General Mladic. I hadn't seen Ratko Mladic before. When I reached the free territory in Tuzla and I saw him on TV, I was 100 per cent sure that it was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that when he addressed you -- well, in doing so, did he insult any of people assembled there?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: No. He came at dusk, and he said, Good evening, neighbours. And we said, Good evening. He told us the governments are in negotiations and tomorrow you will be exchanged all for all. We said, Thank you, commander and we applauded. After that he said, You will go to the hangars, you will have water, but there will be no dinner. After he left, I don't know if it was an order or not, but the first row started boarding the vehicles and the second and the third, and when it was my turn to go, I went down to the truck and they told us, get on the trailer. It was the kind of truck which transports raw materials from mines with high trailers and sides. I saw a young man in uniform, perhaps around 30, with a goatee and a black Serbian cap with the kokarde, and he said, I will go with this one, meaning with this vehicle, and the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To go back to the movement of the column before the surrender, I omitted a question. Did you see any people in the column committing suicide?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Up there in the forest, I saw a man kill himself. It was not en route, but when we were up there and while they were inviting us to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that, you were transported to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Today you said the soldiers shouted out names and took some people away.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: No, not soldiers. People would approach a bus or a truck and ask if there were people -- people from Bljecevo, Potocari, Glogova or Usmolici [phoen]. If somebody responded they asked for his name and his father's name and then they would take him away. When we arrived there, there was a driver who was driving some supplies up to the people. He had a truck without registration plates. I -- he said it was from a Vihor garage. I don't know even know whether that is the case. In any case, on one side there were garages and on the others some buildings. When we arrived there, a boy peaked through the curtains and an elderly woman shooed him away. When they took people away we could hear blunt blows and moans, and then they would say, Stop it, stop it. And one could hear a burst of fire and it all fell silent. It went like that throughout the night. I don't know how late in the evening or at night it was, but a Serb soldier approached our truck and asked if there were people from Srebrenica. There was a man sitting in the nearest corner to him and who got up and he said, I am. The question was, What village were you from. And the man answered, From Ljeskovik. And he didn't want him to take him away.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last short sentence. We did not catch it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the last short sentence that you gave right at the end of your answer. Could you please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that a question for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] yes. You said: "There was a man sitting in the nearest corner nearest to him and who got up and he said, I am." And then "want to take him away." We don't know -- you didn't finish that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That man, since he was quite close to the trailer, that man was close to the soldier and when he asked if there was someone from Srebrenica, the man said, I am. And I know the man by his first and last name. I used to know him. He asked him from what village he was, and he said from Ljeskovik, so it means that they didn't want any people from that village. He told him to sit down and the same man ended up in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your view, how many people were taken away in Bratunac, in that way?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Maybe 100 or 200. I have no idea. It lasted the whole night. They didn't take people dozen by dozen, but one by one. Some were hit with rifle-butts. One of them was being told that he would have to sing the songs from an entire cassette tape. I have no idea what cassette tape they were talking about, and I don't know who the man was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you left Bratunac, could you hear someone shouting that they should wait for UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you waited another two or three hours at the place they said UNPROFOR should be waited for, so you were stopped and waited a few hours?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Well, we waited for maybe two, three, four hours. In any case, it was long. It was very hot. The sides of the trailer were made of metal and luckily the driver brought us some food as well, some water as well. A boy of 15 or 16 from Bratunac who brought us some water too. He was quite well built and he asked for Ismet Ramic, who was a shoemaker from Bratunac. The people wanted to know why he was looking for that man, and the boy answered, He is my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did UNPROFOR representatives show up?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you about the moment of your arrival in Orahovac at the Grbovci school; correct?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes, some call it Orahovac, other Grbovci. That's how people refer to it. I used to know it as Grbovci rather than Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the gym where you were put in, all of the people were seated on the floor; correct?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Among you there were four boys; correct?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: Yes. The boys were separated. Closest to the door. They were given a blanket, whereas the rest of us were not. In my view, one of them was so young that he wasn't older than 10. Judging by his stature, he was about 10 years old, whereas, there was another boy of 11 who weighed as much as 60 kilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened with the boys?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: When I reached the free territory, I asked whether four children had been released, and they said that they had. If not, I can tell you that they were killing everyone from 10 to 70 years of age. I know a neighbour of mine from my village who was 70. And there may have been older people than that whom I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did not count the people in the gym.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The people who guarded you in the Orahovac gym, did they introduce themselves?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: The ones that stood at the door with the weapons that were very young, most of them held rifles like this. When someone spoke to them, saying, soldier, they would respond, We are not soldiers. We are Karadzic's Chetniks. It's just that we don't have any beards. They were all very young, and I don't think that they could grown beards, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you didn't know who those people guarding you belonged to.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: They belonged to the Serbs. Who else? They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't formulate the question quite properly. Did you know what unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: No, we didn't. We were not familiar with any particular unit of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's now go forward in time, in 1999, when you were on-site with Mr. Ruez. Would you agree with me that, at that point in time, you did not manage to locate the execution site. Mr. Ruez took you there.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: I did recognise the location. It's just that -- well, I don't know where exactly I lay. In any case, on the other side of the railroad there was a corn field. I ran through the corn field. When we came to the location, the corn had already been reaped, and only stalks were left, swaying in the wind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what are you saying? Could you or could you not recognise the location?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: I recognised it. But, Mr. Lukic, let me tell you this: If I blindfold you, if I put you under a tarpaulin on a truck and let you out somewhere you had never been before and then bring you back four years later, you wouldn't recognise it either. I never saw it before. I only saw it from the other side of the railroad from the corn field. I was brought there blindfolded under a tarpaulin, and you wouldn't know either, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am not blaming you for anything. I'm just asking whether you would agree that you couldn't recognise the location when you went there with Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: I recognised the location. But I never saw that plot with my bare eyes until then and even when I took off the blindfold, it was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case we'll have to bring up 1D955. We had some problems with e-court yesterday, and that is why we split the transcript in two parts. This is the second part. 1D955. We need page 798, which is page 5 in e-court, in the second part. We're interested in lines 23 through 25, as well as line 1 on the next page. I apologise. It must be the first part of the document, and we're interested in page 783. That is to say, page 5 in the first part. Yes, lines 23 through 25. I'll read it out in English: [In English] "Q. And my last question is that when you visited the sites where the shootings took place -- and that was -- this question was asked by my colleague -- but you did not recognise those sites, did you?" Answer on the next page --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I recognised the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "A. Yes, because I was blindfolded."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I recognised it. After I fled I crossed the rail tracks and there was immediately a corn field there. When we came to the site, as I told you, one could still hear the stalks of the corn in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your testimony in the Popovic case on the 25th of August, when you were asked whether it is true that you didn't recognise the location, you said: "Yes, because I was blindfolded. When I was brought there, the only thing I could see were the dead in front of me."

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: No. When we were brought there to be executed, my group, when I looked in front of me, at my feet, I saw a dead man. I have three children, and they immediately came to my mind. I thought I would never see them again. And I started praying to God to die as a religious man, not a atheist, and I could only ponder and picture death at that moment. Fear is not great at such a point in time. People about to be executed are not all that afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just before we break for the day, tell me this, please: Are you telling us that what you said in the Popovic trial was not correct?

utterances.speaker: RM297
utterances.text: No, no. Perhaps I did say it. I'm not saying I didn't. But I know, I'm certain 100 per cent, that that is the location. When I fled across the railroad, the people standing next to the digger fired shots, probably at me, but I didn't -- I wasn't injured. I ran halfway into the field and I thought, Well, the corn is pretty high and, still, they may see me. That's why I went down to my knees. I went through the corn field, came out to the back, and there was a small forest there where I could hear water running, but I couldn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It is time to conclude for the day, and we'll have to continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Witness, we have to break for the day. You'll have to come back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. May we -- we are just going to adjourn now. But before we do that, can we ask that the -- go into closed session for you to leave the court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Well, we stand adjourned to tomorrow, Friday, the 10th of May, in Courtroom III at 9.30. Court adjourned.
